blocks.text: Expanding brackets is like unpacking a bag — everything spreads out. Factorising is packing it back neatly. Almost every quadratic question in WAEC, NECO and JAMB starts with a candidate who can factorise quickly and confidently.

blocks.markdown:
**Expanding** means removing brackets by multiplying out. **Factorising** means putting the brackets back — writing an expression as a product.

They are exact opposites, so you can always check a factorisation by expanding it again. That check is free marks.

blocks.title: Factor
blocks.text: A factor is something that divides exactly into an expression. To factorise is to write the expression as a product of its factors, for example $6x + 9 = 3(2x + 3)$.

steps.text: Multiply every term in the first bracket by every term in the second.
Work out each product, watching the signs carefully.
Collect the two like terms in the middle.

blocks.markdown:
### Method 1: highest common factor

Always look for a common factor **first**. Take out the largest number and the lowest power of each letter that appears in every term.

For $12a^2b - 8ab^2$ the common factor is $4ab$, leaving $4ab(3a - 2b)$. A factorisation is only complete when the bracket has no common factor left.

### Method 2: difference of two squares

If you see one square **subtract** another square, the factorisation is instant:

$$a^2 - b^2 = (a - b)(a + b)$$

So $x^2 - 49 = (x - 7)(x + 7)$. Note that $a^2 + b^2$ does **not** factorise — the minus sign is essential.

blocks.title: Factorising a harder trinomial by grouping

steps.text: Multiply the first coefficient by the constant.
Find two numbers that multiply to −72 and add to the middle coefficient, −1.
Split the middle term using those two numbers.
The bracket (2x − 3) is now common, so take it out.

blocks.caption: Recognising the pattern is most of the work

blocks.title: Difference of squares as a shortcut
blocks.text: The identity works on numbers too. $87^2 - 13^2 = (87 - 13)(87 + 13) = 74 \times 100 = 7400$, which you can do in your head. Examiners set this deliberately to reward students who spot the structure.

points: Expanding and factorising are inverse processes, so always check by expanding back.
Take out the highest common factor before trying anything else.
$a^2 - b^2 = (a - b)(a + b)$, but $a^2 + b^2$ does not factorise.
For a trinomial, find two numbers that multiply to $ac$ and add to $b$, then split the middle term.
A factorisation is not finished while a bracket still contains a common factor.
